At hatching, neonates display a precocial profile, with a wet weight at birth of roughly 12 grams [Wwb = roughly 12 grams], a modest mass that reflects the energetically efficient yolk-to-tissue conversion characteristic of this lineage. Before the onset of exogenous feeding, the initial wet weight of the newly hatched chick is recorded at 17 grams [Ww0 = 17 grams], representing the total mass of the chick including residual yolk reserves. This initial mass provides a crucial energetic buffer during the first days post-hatch, when the chick must rapidly develop thermoregulatory capacity and begin foraging alongside its parents. The relatively small birth mass, compared to the adult body size, underscores the substantial growth trajectory that lies ahead for the developing bird.

Under captive conditions designed to approximate the thermal environment of the species' native Guam savannas (40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]), fledging—the achievement of sustained flight—occurs at 23 days after hatching [tx = 23 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone is notably rapid for a rail of this body size, likely an adaptation to evade introduced predators. The attainment of sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gametogenesis, follows considerably later: puberty is reached at 69 days after hatching [tp = 69 days after hatching] when maintained at this same elevated temperature at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C].

Adult body mass in the Guam rail exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism. Published reports (Taylor, 2020) indicate a broader range of 170 to 274 grams for adult body mass, reflecting variation across seasons and individual condition. This dimorphism in mass, with males averaging roughly ten percent heavier than females, is consistent with a mating system characterized by male-male competition for territories and access to mates. The larger male body size likely confers advantages in aggressive encounters and in defense of nesting sites from conspecifics and potential predators, a critical trait for a ground-nesting species on an island with limited refuge options.

First reproduction in the Guam rail occurs approximately one year after hatching, representing a life-history strategy that balances the risks of extended juvenile mortality against the benefits of delayed breeding. Under the thermal regime of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], the time since birth at first brood is recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days]. This reproductive delay is typical of island rails, which often exhibit slower life-history paces than their mainland counterparts. The species' maximum reproductive output is achieved through repeated nesting efforts: females typically lay 3.5 eggs per season [Ri = 3.5 eggs per season], distributed across 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2 clutches per year]. This annual reproductive investment is relatively modest compared to continental rail species, reflecting the constraints of a stable but resource-limited island environment where adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity.

Longevity data for the Guam rail, derived from captive populations, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8.5 years [am = approximately 8.5 years] when maintained at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to about 3100 days [am = about 3100 days], is notable for a bird of its body size and aligns with the 'slow' life-history syndrome observed in many oceanic island species, where reduced predation pressure and stable resource availability favor increased survival at the expense of high reproductive output at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. The contrast between this longevity and the modest annual fecundity—a total of approximately 7 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 7 eggs per year] across two clutches—illustrates a classic life-history trade-off. The species' historical decline in the wild, driven primarily by predation from introduced brown tree snakes, was likely exacerbated by this slow reproductive rate, as the population could not compensate for elevated adult mortality. Conservation breeding programs have successfully leveraged the species' capacity for multiple clutches under controlled conditions.
